newsitem.title: INDIA: India's pathbreaking budget hangs in balance.
newsitem.headline: India's pathbreaking budget hangs in balance.

text.p: India's parliament has agreed to take up the nation's pathbreaking federal budget next week, but it was unclear if the political crisis and amendments would blunt its thrust, polticians said on Monday.
"Most probably amendments will come from various parties, some consensus will come," Congress party spokesman Vithal Gadgil told Reuters.

The tax-cutting 1997/98 (April-March) budget, which sparked a stock market rally after it was unveiled on February 28, has been held hostage by a two-week political crisis that now appears to be coming to a head.

Last week, stock markets took heart in the news that despite the political uncertainty sparked by the fall of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government, political parties agreed to consider the budget in a special session from April 21 to 23.

The United Front coalition's plan to cut taxes and boost investment has been welcomed by businessmen as a way to spurr industry. The budget, which would slash taxes and import duties, has drawn widespread support from the public.
Gadgil said Congress, which provoked the fall of Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition on Friday by withdrawing support, has not yet decided on the amendments that it will move.
"The shape (of the budget) could change," Gadgil said. "The scenario is different now."

The budget, presented to parliament by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, has been held over from the ousted United Front government and needs to be passed by parliament before its provisions can take effect.
"What we have agreed to is the budget will be discussed fully," said Somnath Chatterjee, leader of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) in the lower house, the Lok Sabha.
Chatterjee told Reuters that while he did not expect the budget to be rejected, his party planned to move amendments. He did not elaborate on the amendments.

"I take it some provisions of the finance bill could be changed." Chatterjee said, referring to the tax and tariff bill. "The question is what amendments, who is moving (them) and the nature of support for it."
The appropriation bill, already examined by a parliamentary panel, lists the demands for grants or the spending proposals of the various ministries.
Chatterjee said that before the fall of Deve Gowda's government, there was an understanding among parties on the budget but the situation no longer prevailed.
Newspapers said the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), with the largest number of deputies in the Lok Sabha, had set up a committee to examine the budget.
They said the BJP might press for higher customs duties to protect domestic industry and for higher standard deductions for lower income taxpayers.
But it was not clear how sweeping the Congress or BJP amendments might be.

Analysts said the readiness shown by different political parties to discuss the finance bill was a silver lining in an overwise cloudy political picture. No party wants to risk public anger by blocking the budget.
The fine print could be significantly altered by amendments, although no one expects the plan to be emasculated.
"Everything is fluid. Everything is in flux," said Chatterjee.
